candidates.title: BPR-0975: a WSLg-only workaround (A), wait for WSLg (B), or both?
criteria: BPR-0975 AC2 cannot pass on WSLg as the product and WSLg stand. Which do you choose: A, a WSLg-only workaround in the product; B, no product change, with the card Blocked until WSLg ships the upstream fix; or both A and B?
options: A. WSLg-only workaround: on X11 under WSLg, hide and re-show a reused inactive Settings window, and on close return focus to the workbench that last opened it
B. No product change: the card goes to Blocked until a WSLg release ships the upstream activation fix
Both: make the workaround (A) now, and also keep waiting on the upstream fix (B)
Other: my answer is in the note
candidates.content:
Why it fails. WSLg's compositor (weston-mirror 04d436c7, WSLg 1.0.73.2) never activates a window because an application asked. Its X11 window manager drops _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW unread (xwayland/window-manager.c 2217-2247) whatever the source or timestamp, and puts X11 focus back when a client moves it (2606-2631). It offers no xdg_activation_v1 to Wayland clients. Its shell activates a window only on a click, when Windows activates the window's RAIL window, when a window maps, or when the focused window goes away. Qt's request is already the one EWMH asks for. No setting changes this, and switching the application to Wayland would not help. microsoft/wslg#1022 reports the same defect.

The probe (2026-09-24T20:43:58Z-20:44:34Z, desktop hold acknowledged by bpr-main-win, guard 8/8 live files unchanged, every control exit 0): every activation request was refused (Xlib with source 0, 1 or 2 and any timestamp; XSetInputFocus undone; Qt activateWindow() on xcb and Wayland). The only thing that moved focus, in every control, was unmapping the window and mapping it again. The Windows foreground followed each time.

A. A WSLg-only workaround. It is not an activation request; it relies on WSLg activating a window when it maps. When Ctrl-comma or the menu reuses a visible Settings window that is not active, the product hides and shows it before raising it. Windows destroys and recreates its window, so the taskbar button blinks and the window flickers; the Qt window and its X11 identity stay the same. On close, Settings returns focus to the workbench that last opened or reused it (today it asks for the first opener, which WSLg refuses when a sibling was used later). Both changes apply to xcb under WSLg only. Expected, not yet shown: the full course then passes; that needs the implementation, the Settings suites and another desktop hold.

B. No product change. The card goes to Blocked until a WSLg release ships the upstream change. AC2 stays failing on WSLg until then. The other desktop and the amendment were rejected on 2026-09-24, so B leaves the card waiting.

Both: make A now and keep the upstream fix as the lasting remedy. Whether to report the upstream change is the next, separate item.

candidates.title: BPR-0975: prepare an upstream report for microsoft/wslg#1022?
candidates.revision: 2e6e64d4 (the upstream change text in the BPR-0975 evidence note)
criteria: Should an upstream report for microsoft/wslg#1022 be prepared from the change text already written in the BPR-0975 evidence note? Yes or no.
options: Yes: prepare the report for microsoft/wslg#1022 from the prepared text
No: do not prepare it
Other: my answer is in the note
candidates.content:
microsoft/wslg#1022 (Emacs other-frame cannot switch frames, open since 2023-03) reports the same defect. Nothing has been filed. The prepared text, section "The upstream change that would fix it" of the evidence note, proposes four changes to microsoft/weston-mirror (and upstream Weston, which shares the X11 window manager):
1. xwayland/window-manager.c: handle _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW in weston_wm_handle_client_message and hand the window, source and timestamp to the shell, which makes its _NET_SUPPORTED advertisement true.
2. xwayland/xwayland-internal-interface.h: a request_activate entry, implemented by libweston-desktop through a new optional activation_requested callback.
3. rdprail-shell/shell.c: register activation_requested and activate the surface behind a focus-stealing rule (grant a pager request; grant an application request when the client owns the focused surface or its timestamp is no older than that surface's last input).
4. For Wayland clients: an xdg_activation_v1 global in the RAIL shell calling the same activate(); Qt 6.11.2 uses it with no application change.

This item asks only whether to prepare the report. Preparing it posts nothing: filing it on GitHub stays your call, as the card says. This question is independent of the A/B choice in the previous item.

candidates.title: BPR-0974: the Defender disposition, now that BPR-1110 explains it
candidates.revision: BPR-1110 finding at 94a09016 (finished 657ca3bb); threat 2147731250 on source 2d3bdbdf
criteria: With BPR-1110's explanation (a first-run cloud machine-learning verdict on a new, unsigned, reputation-less image), which dispositions do you authorize for the Bearfoos.A!ml finding? Tick every one you want; anything else goes in the note.
options: Authenticode-sign the Windows images (OV/EV certificate or a managed signing service; release work under RFC-0038/BPR-0960, needs your certificate)
Lower the static signals: add a VERSIONINFO resource, keep a PDB reference in Release (/PDBALTPATH:%_PDB%), and move the 3.6 MB of compressed resource blobs out of the executable
Submit the quarantined sample to Microsoft as a false positive (an external disclosure of an unreleased binary; clears that hash only)
Build a fresh tests-disabled image and scan it on demand; if Defender does not detect it, run that exact digest for AC2/AC3
Defer the disposition to RFC-0038's release-security qualification (BPR-0960/BPR-0962) and keep BPR-0974 Blocked
Other: my answer is in the note
candidates.content:
Your note last time: "Explain why this is being triggered." BPR-1110 did, read-only, on the Windows station:
1. Defender recognised nothing in the program. The image sat on disk about three minutes undetected. Within about three seconds of its first launch, Microsoft's cloud sent a new signature made for this one file (event 2010, dynamic signature compiled that second) and Defender quarantined both copies. !ml marks a machine-learning verdict; FastPath marks a cloud-delivered dynamic signature. It is a model classifying a never-seen file, not a match against known malware.
2. Nothing the program does changed. An unflagged tests-disabled Release sibling (M9 67f5e514, same host, compiler, Qt and preset, 4.5 hours earlier) has the same 2,889 imports from 22 DLLs and the same resources; section sizes differ by 16 and 8 bytes; src/ differs by a 6-line shortcut change.
3. Why a model might call it a trojan (inference): unsigned, no version information, no debug path, no reputation; 3.6 MB of near-random data (the compressed Qt resources, about 28% of the file); and an import list combining Credential Manager, token and ACL editing, a child process started suspended, and a network client. The product needs each; together they look like a credential stealer.
4. The verdict is per file and probabilistic. A new build is a new unknown file. Only an Authenticode signature, with the reputation it builds, changes that reliably. The static-signal changes lower the risk without removing it.

Until you choose, nothing is restored, excluded, rebuilt around, executed or disclosed. BPR-0653's Windows capture needs the same kind of tests-disabled image, so its capture build waits on this answer. BPR-1110 also lists linking as a GUI-subsystem program (WIN32_EXECUTABLE), a weak signal that changes console behaviour; name it in the note if you want it.

candidates.title: BPR-1109 (optional): the Alt-chord keyboard hook on JaegAW: known owner, find it, or ignore?
criteria: Optional. Something on JaegAW rewrites the Alt of an Alt chord typed fast. Do you know which program owns the hook, do you want the quit-one-at-a-time procedure to find it, or should it be ignored?
options: I know which program it is (named in the note)
Give me the quit-one-at-a-time procedure to find it
Ignore it
Other: my answer is in the note
candidates.content:
Informational; skipping it is fine and leaves nothing blocked.

What it is: a low-level keyboard hook intercepts an Alt press that another key follows at once and replaces the Alt with key code 0, so the application sees the key without Alt. It keys on timing: back-to-back Alt chords are rewritten; the same key 47-57 ms after the Alt passes. Human typing mostly will not notice; scripted input and fast chords do.

Candidates (interactive-session processes running at both observations whose loaded code imports SetWindowsHookExW): msrdc (WSLg's Remote Desktop client), ChatGPT/Codex and its codex-computer-use runtime, the NVIDIA overlay, Everything, Slack, Discord, Chrome, Visual Studio (with Visual Assist), OneDrive, and the Windows shell (explorer, taskbar, text input host). Station automation, exited processes and the restarted Claude desktop are ruled out.

The procedure: you quit one candidate at a time, and the station reruns BPR-1022's one-minute check (a back-to-back Alt+Space) after each. The check is the station's; stopping applications is yours.

candidates.title: BPR-0644: remembered sign-in material that signs in as a different account
criteria: When the material in a remembered sign-in turns out to sign in as a different GitHub account than the one remembered, should BetterPullReview (a) keep erasing it at once, as the one automatic removal, or (b) keep it until you sign out, like every other failure?
options: (a) Keep erasing it at once: the one automatic removal
(b) Keep it until I sign out, like every other failure
Other: my answer is in the note
candidates.content:
Your rule from last time: a remembered grant is removed only when you remove it in Settings. It is built (1347f776): a locked or denied Keychain, a network failure, an expired access token, and a refused, spent or expired refresh token all keep the grant; the card says it needs signing in again and offers Begin and Sign out. No security reason to erase dead refresh material was found.

One case still erases on its own: material that signs in as an account the binding never named. Two paths reach it: a launch renewal whose rotated grant's /user answers another account, and a restored access slot whose /user answers another account. The session is refused in both, as before, and both slots are erased. The reason: otherwise the slot keeps a live credential for someone else under a key that names your own account. Nothing would use it, but it would stay on the machine.

candidates.title: BPR-1107 (2 of 2): the White space setting's six choices and its default
criteria: Do you accept the White space row's six choices (None, Under the selection, Leading, Trailing, Leading and trailing, All) with Under the selection as the default?
options: Accept the six choices, default Under the selection (proposed; Sublime's own default)
Accept the six choices, default Trailing instead
Other: my answer is in the note
candidates.content:
One row on the Appearance page's Type card, White space, directly beneath Tab width. It chooses when white space is drawn:
None: nothing.
Under the selection (proposed default; Sublime's ["selection"]): every white space character on a selected line.
Leading: indentation.
Trailing: from the last other character to the end of the line.
Leading and trailing: both, so also a line of white space alone (Sublime's "isolated").
All: everything, enclosed white space too.

Left out, and why: combining choices (one at a time keeps the row one line); enclosed and isolated alone (All and Leading and trailing cover them); the _tabs, _spaces and _none refinements (they would triple the list); the _mixed refinements (the review window has no indentation style); indentation guides (a separate setting, not white space). The setting persists per profile (appearance store version 8). Section 2 of the design page shows each choice in Light and Dark.

media.label: The Type card, Light: White space beneath Tab width
Under the selection (the reader on the first line), Light

candidates.title: BPR-1106: where Compose review and Draft comment or reply go
criteria: Where do Compose review and Draft comment or reply go? A, keep the row as it is; B, the strip's review menu; C, the right end of the Updates line (the loading line moves into it too); D, the foot of the conversation drawer; or E, a Compose control in the strip. Proposed: C.
options: A. Keep the row as it is (baseline)
B. The strip's review menu
C. The right end of the Updates line; the loading line moves into it too (proposed)
D. The foot of the conversation drawer
E. A Compose control in the strip
Other: my answer is in the note
candidates.content:
Your note last time asked for a UX design round on where these entries go. The design page holds the five placements at a glance and close up, their costs to scale, and 50 frames.

What each costs:
A: 22 px of comparison height on macOS, 20 on Windows and Linux, every mode; 1 click each.
B: no height, no strip width; 2 clicks each; Alt+Shift+4 then C or D; both entries hidden in a menu.
C: no height, no strip width; 1 click each; takes 303 px of the Updates line's track (1000 becomes 697 at 1280); the readiness wording and bar take the track's place while loading, so no row comes or goes.
D: no height (the drawer's thread column gives 36); 1 click, or 2 with the drawer hidden.
E: +59 px of Windows strip width at its 902 floor (floor to 961 or a new yield); 1 click to compose, 2 to draft.

Proposed: C (the comparison gets its pixels back, nothing is added to the Windows strip, each entry keeps one click and a visible label, and the readiness line gets a home that does not move the window when loading ends). Runner-up D. B is cheapest to build but hides both entries. E spends width the Windows strip does not have.

If you pick B, C, D or E, RFC-BPR-0028 AC-01 and its chrome paragraph are amended again and the implementation is carded (with BPR-1036's floor and BPR-0940's window assertion). The close-ups below are macOS dark at 1280; the page has every placement at both sizes, light and dark, macOS and Windows.

C: the Updates line's right end (proposed)
